A Shared Redis Connection →

Queues and Workers

BullMQ's two halves — a Queue that adds jobs, a Worker that processes them — and why splitting them into separate processes is the whole point.

BullMQ splits "schedule this" from "do this" into two separate objects, both backed by the same Redis instance so either one can be created in a process that never sees the other:

  • A Queue adds jobs. Calling queue.add(name, data, options) writes a job into Redis — that call returns as soon as the write is done, whether or not anything is currently listening to process it.
  • A Worker processes jobs. new Worker(queueName, processorFn, options) connects to that same Redis instance, watches for jobs on that queue, and calls processorFn for each one as it arrives.

Nothing requires the Queue and the Worker to live in the same process — in fact the usual reason to reach for BullMQ at all is so they don't. This project's SLA monitor puts the Queue half in the API process (it just needs to say "run a scan periodically") and the Worker half in a brand new process this lesson introduces, src/worker.js, started separately with its own npm run worker script. If the worker process is down, jobs still queue up in Redis and get picked up the moment it comes back — the crash-loses- everything problem from the previous slide, solved by not keeping any of this state in a process's memory in the first place.

BullMQ also handles retries for you: a Worker's processor function that throws gets the job retried automatically, with a configurable delay between attempts (backoff) — precisely the "silent failure" problem a bare setInterval has no answer for. The next slide sets up the one thing both halves need before either can be created: a connection to Redis itself.
